author: @tys3838

text:
Depends on what you're after, honestly. For me, the 5700XT definitely seemed like a better value per buck, but I really didn't want to experience any driver issues, wanted slightly cooler operation and lower power usage (my PSU tends to get loud at high usage) so went with an 2060S instead. Also, what other people have said, nvenc is apparently loads better of an encoder than what AMD offers right now, if that matters to you any.
As for raytracing, I didn't really buy it for that as that technology still needs much more performance to be useful in games, but it's a nice tech demo to get to try out as a bonus. Looks nice in Quake 2 RTX, but if you're simply looking for performance in games and can get a 5700XT card with proper cooling, if you can live with AMDs questionable drivers, I'd kinda recommend that. In the end, it's really up to you and the pricing of the two brands in your region, I don't think you can go wrong with either.

author: @Rafaelzp3

text:
If you can get a 5700 XT with a decent cooler that does not get loud and depending on the prices in your region, the 5700 XT is a good purchase. I bought an 2060S myself, primarily due to more stable drivers, lower thermals and power usage (my noise driver in gaming is actually my 750W PSU at this point).
If you need video encoding (like streaming), nvenc is still apparently miles better than AMDs offering. 



You can't go wrong with either board, really, with the caveat that nvidia drivers apparently still seem to be more stable at this point. For me, that alone was worth a slight price premium because I didn't want to experience the frustration of potentially wonky drivers. Not sure what the state of AMD drivers are at the moment, I've heard someone say they've actually gotten worse since 2016 so your mileage may vary. My previous 2 GPUs were also nvidia and I haven't had any issues with them so that also kinda biased my choice. If your previous GPU was AMD as well, I'd weight that in on the expectation of driver stability over my opinion. Good luck on your new purchase either way!

text: ​ @MyGunGoesBooom  Arrived yesterday, using it with a 144hz 34' monitor from LG 34UC79G, it's 1080 but UW, the experience in Apex, Dota2, War Thunder, CS GO and some other games like Path of Exile It's a total BLAST. All the features added up, good response time, stable fps, freesync and big gaming monitor actually ensured me 1/1 win in Apex and being the kill lead (which never happened before, 14 kills). About the card I can only say so far that it's a total BEAST. I didn't used OC yet, just got it so Im still testing things at this point. Using driver 19.10.9. Also few days ago I got an 3900x CPU with M.2 970 Evo 1TB, 16GB ram 3600mhz cl 16. Upgraded from an FX 8350, 8 gb ram DDR3, with an old mobo. The difference was about 5 to 15 fps. BTW your graphs for PCIe 4.0 were completely broken.. all the bards were 100% rather than varying slightly one was even off by 6% It's also worth nothing that GDDR6 is a $ vs Power tradoff... you get a cheaper but lower performing card, for the big GPU it will likely cost a little more but have HBM3 meaning higher bandwith and much less power wasted per bit transfered meaning more power to spend on rendering probably to the tune of 10-15% just from that aspect alone.

text:
Really hoping the driver issues will be fixed and a decent partner board with a twin fan cooler wouldn't rack up the price too much. The value proposition based on these results is quite good. I gathered up the lowest price components on a local price hunting site, and got these results for various Nvidia vs. AMD price and performance comparisons:

RTX 2060 vs. RX 5700 = Radeon 5.5% more expensive & 12.5% faster
RTX 2060 Super vs. RX 5700 = Radeon 23% cheaper &  0.27% slower

RTX 2060 Super vs. RX 5700 XT = Radeon 11.1% cheaper & 8.5% faster

RTX 2070 vs. RX 5700 XT = Radeon 4.3% cheaper & 2.1% faster

RTX 2070 Super vs. RX 5700 XT = Radeon 31.5% cheaper & 6.7% slower

RX 5700 vs. RX 5700 XT = XT 15.4% more expensive &  8.7% faster


So the RX 5700 is like a 2060 Super (minus ray tracing and Nvidia's better software package) at almost 1/4th cheaper, and the RX 5700 XT is essentially like a slightly faster and cheaper 2070, beating the 2060 Super in both performance and price. Also not that massively behind the 2070 Super considering it's almost 1/3rd cheaper. Prices will vary of course, I just checked what was cheapest for me.


Interesting that the 2060 Super is a significantly worse deal than the 2070 over here atm., being about 5.9% slower than while being 7.7% more expensive. Admittedly the 2070 I found was a pretty poor quality card and on sale, a "decent one" would have cost about 8.8% more than the 2060 Super. With that pricing though the RX 5700 XT would be an even better deal at 18.2% cheaper and 2.1% faster.

text:
The die sizes for these new Navi cards are pretty small, they definitely have a lot of room to flesh this architecture out in a higher end card. TDP might start to become an issue as it did with the Vega line but that's more on a "case by case" basis (take the pun if you'd like). They don't NEED to resort to liquid cooling but I wouldn't be surprised to see a $1500+ variant of whatever the top end card ends up being with a LC block attached. 

You guys should def use the phantom for that, sounds like a good video. Another cool idea would be to use single variable adjustments on a PC to determine which parts of a system are the most important to spend your money on getting something with "low lag" compared to its competitors. 

Like I would say getting 3 choices in each category would be ideal; one budget buy that just shoots for something passable for as little money as possible, one balanced pick that offers a good price to performance ratio, and one final product that is very to prohibitively expensive but claims to be the best/significantly better for the extra cash. You'd need a product from each of those categories for a mouse, keyboard, a monitor, and you could even throw in a few GPUs to see if how much of an impact spending more there has on lag.

From there just test them all and maybe conclude with a comparison chart that not only shows how each "tier" of product compares outright with each other and in terms of value per dollar but also compare the ultimate millisecond shaved to dollar spent ratio with all the products regardless of category to see if what part of a rig gives the most noticable difference when upgrading/purchasing vs others.

I wouldn't be surprised to find out that a really good gaming mouse (around say $75-$100) with low latency/lag makes a bigger performance difference vs a cheap/ancient mouse than a $400 1ms monitor has over a cheapo one with maybe 7-10ms of response time and some additional input lag. Itd be interesting to know for sure what is the absolute most ideal place to spend your money to make the biggest difference if responsiveness is all you're after.

text:
Why does everybody still think Radeon Image Sharpening and Fidelity FX are the same thing? They're not. RIS is a simple sharpening filter applied at a driver level, so of course it's going to look great in some instances and poor in others, it's a blanket feature. Fidelity FX is a game engine utility that will offer optimisation and tuning for best performance.


So please stop saying Fidelity FX is touch and go when you've not actually seen it run yet.

text:
The card runs hot because of the cheap heatsink to save a few bucks.... The Laws of Thermodynamics still applies here, the arch can easily be scaled up. The Cards are close to Nvidia's in terms of power usage and there is a lot of room left in terms of power draw a big card can handle. 


AMD has never used an expensive blower cooler on their cards. Pretty much any decent dual fan cooler will keep this card nice and cool. Honestly a big win for AMD, with a better cooler the 5700xt will be very competitive.


Honestly Nvidia's software stack is not that impressive, granted the LTT group has always been nvidia biased. As a Nvidia gtx1080 user, the software stack does nothing that my old r9 290 couldn't do. That is actually worth while for game use. RTX in its first implementation is really weak. It was like buying a 6800ultra for shader model 3, sure a few games with SM3 would work fine on the 6800ultra. But by the time SM3 became common, the 6800ultra could not even keep up. This is how the Current RTX cards are going to be, by the time Ray Tracing is more common place the current RTX cards won't handle it, and will have to turn the feature off. Already Ray Tracing is a struggle, next gen Ray Tracing hardware is going to make nvidia's first attempt a waste of space that will only be good for the first few games that supported it. Everything else will cripple the cards so much to make it worthless.  I'm actually liking the Hybrid idea AMD is going to use for Raytracing, hopefully Nvidia goes down this route as well. 


Based on the new benchmarks, a new high end AMD card could easily match/exceed nvidia's best. But question is how long will it take to show up. AMD needs to hurry up on delivery times. 


I don't see why someone wanting pure gaming performance for the next couple of years wouldn't go AMD over Nvidia. More performance for the same $$, win win to me. RTX is a worthless option, and will only ever be useful for the few first gen raytracing games. I want to like it, but the performance just isn't there on their midrage cards.

text:
ANTI-LAG
I have SERIOUS doubts that this works as advertised. Also, NVidia apparently has had this for a while, but somehow they demo'd one "example" where they supposedly beat NVidia? Hey, if I'm wrong then great. I just also understand how VSYNC works so what they are advertising seems overly optimistic. Somehow they throttle the CPU (draw calls?) so it "doesn't get too far ahead of the GPU" or whatever. Why that isn't already synchronized is a little baffling to me but okay. Also, they focus on the "button press to photon display" which is the full input lag but the main issue with GPU lag has to do with VSYNC buffering, missed frames etc so gaining a few milliseconds is insignificant for lag so it's more about VSYNC (AFAIK)... anyway, I need a better explanation because something doesn't quite add up... here's my questions then:
1) VSYNC only? (I don't see why VSYNC OFF, or Freesync would use this if each frame is started right after the next one)
2) TYPICAL benefit?
3) How does NVidia compare now? (I'm betting it's the same)
4) HOW exactly does it work?
5) Does this aid Crossfire X or whatever they call Crossfire now? (multi-GPU has major pacing issues synchronizing both GPU's. NVidia's improved this a lot but not just through software but also recently with NVLink for supports RTX2000 cards... I don't recommend multi-GPU but it's still a question)

text:
DSC
Just FYI, but DSC also requires the MONITOR support DSC. It's a non-issue for 2560x1440 monitors as they should support up to 200Hz with full 10-bit 4:4:4 sampling. However, for 4K monitors you'll want 4K or you'll be limited to 98Hz (98FPS) if you want 10-bit 4:4:4. My point is you can BUY any modern graphics card and it should have DSC (AFAIK) but you might want to hold off on the monitor. On a side note if you want an HDR monitor get one with HDR1000. If it's HDR600 or lower don't factor that into the value and just DISABLE it. HDR is either an improvement or it's making things worse. HDR1000 should be the minimum (and some of that is achieved with FALD which has it's own issues but I don't want to go too far off topic). OLED once sorted for desktop would be ideal.

text:
PRODUCTIVITY
Wendel's buddy from another site (I don't know his name) said the 5700XT beat the RTX2080Ti in certain productivity HOWEVER he speculated that may be due to the increase PCIe v4.0 bandwidth. Obviously he should retest using a non-X570 motherboard with only PCIe v3.0 but that's all I can report so far... my point is if you are into productivity you should investigate that. It won't change the GAMING situation, but the reason SOME productivity eats up the bandwidth is due to the heavy use of the PCIe bus talking back and forth to the CPU/DDR4 etc... but GAMING generally loads textures etc into the on-card VIDEO MEMORY then the GPU talks back and forth to that VRAM with updates over the PCIe bus using much lower bandwidth than certain productivity tasks.

About the fps results in csgo. Please do not use the benchmark from the workshop. 


It is way off compared to real game fps. The avg is a bit higher and the 99th%ile is way way lower.


Why? The benchmark uses parts in which the gpu usage skyrockets 2 times, which are the lows, but these do never happen in an actual game. Neither in competitive or casual. I have a 2070 and the benchmark drops to around 90 fps in the skyrocketing part as well. So the numbers are correct, but don't represent real numbers in actual games AT ALL.


Might be good to compare hardware the fastest way, but it is like someone created a benchmark with the source engine and not a benchmark in csgo. It's not representing real game fps.

text:
Why aren't you talking about dithering support? NVidia drivers support temporal dithering only on Linux, but on Windows they don't, thus forcing people to buy expensive IPS and overlypriced (expeisnve and overpriced are different things) TN panels with 10-12bit matrix. 6-bits TN's cost like 1.5-2times lower and AMD are the good guys here - their software includes dithering support in stock in every OS. Without it the color banding is so fracking bad on NVidia cards that people literally sell their hardware, be it monitors or video cards.
TLDR: with AMD you can buy awesome TN 1ms panel with 6-bit matrix in it for 200 bucks and have exactly the same picture quality as with expensive IPS 4ms (there are no true 1ms IPS panels) or TN with 10-12bit for 500 bucks.
IMO, that should be included in price value.

text:
Great review!! You may have explained the reasoning for AMD cards losing out in the shorter blender benchmarks without realizing ;)
If i am not mistaken, in 3d rendering, simpler scenes are much much easier to scale up across CUs. This is because there's not a whole lot of texture lookup, geometry loading, tessellation etc that goes on. As a result, when one GCN CU is processing essentially four operands one go, its not having to wait for next set of operands. When you have a complex scene, that wait time increases. And RDNA tries to overcome that. If what you're saying is correct, RDNA is essentially less parallel but at much higher frequency. Hence, it wins in complex loads. It will be interesting to see more tests on those. 

Perhaps run even heavier scenes? Like barber shop interior perhaps? It's a part of blender benchmark bundle.
I do understand that would take a whole lot more time because that scene takes a lot longer to render. But if the trend continues there too, then what i am saying is in the ballpark.

2:56


"It can take up to FOUR TIMES LONGER ..."


...should be written/spoken as "...four times as long ..."


Longer = more
More = addition
Four times more = five times as much
1 + (1 * 4) = 1 * 5


This is commonly miscommunicated, but also commonly understood despite the technical incongruence with the literal meaning.


You wouldn't say that 5 is '125% more ' than 4, would you? No, of course not. You would just say '25% more'. But you could say '125% as much '.


It's not that you don't agree, even. It's just more likely that you and everyone you interact with hasn't really bothered to care about it at all. Maybe, next time, do?

text:
Oh, making a higher end card will be easy. The reason it's so hot and power hungry is because it's a tiny little GPU that's been clocked to high heaven. So what you do is make a larger GPU with more compute units, while dropping the clock speed. Mind you, you can only do that once yields improve a bit. That's exactly why we haven't seen it yet though. Also, this is why Nvidia's been slow to move to a smaller manufacturing node. They like making large GPU's. In fact, their entire architecture is kind of dependent on it. But that's harder to do on a newer node with lower yields.

That's why you won't see a proper Turing successor until 2020. It might be fairly late in 2020 at that. Nvidia won't jump on it until they can make them at acceptable yields. The fact that Samsung is giving them a good deal to use their fabs is going to help, but not THAT much. So they'll wait as long as they can. Especially if Turing cards are still selling.

As for this review, well I'd say it's mostly fair and on point. Day 1 AMD drivers are historically a bit iffy. I really wish they'd get over that. Usually, most of the big problems are fixed within a few weeks. So holding off to make a better first impression seems like it would be a really good idea to me! The cards themselves are pretty decent though. We're talking near 1080ti performance for 400usd. That's hard to argue with, and it's probably going to come down in price more in the next six months. After what we've seen in the past six months, I am absolutely expecting a price war now.

It might not start right away mind you. AMD and Nvidia would both have to clear out some existing cards from the market first. Still, once that happens we're probably going to see some actual competition in the market. Which is great. Considering how expensive GPU's have become, we kinda need it.

text:
Another video from the real star of Linus Tech!
I do love your videos, clear, calm, well explained. Possibly a little too 'green' for my liking but I agree you shouldn't buy the reference card but that has been true for almost all reference cards forever, a decent custom cooling solution though will have no issues with the 5700 XT and at the end of the day it's a 1080ti for $399 or a 20% discount on 2070 Super performance. 

In terms of where AMD goes from here, don't worry RDNA will scale really nicely. The 5700 die size is really tiny, I know you don't think these cards were meant to be a Polaris replacement but they really were, proven by the anniversary fan label, but what happened is AMD got greedy. They had a good, solid, quiet, small, low energy chip that would be a big upgrade from the RX590 that they would sell it for $249-299 but they then thought if they tried to clock the hell out of it they could bump the price up to $399-499. That is why it's so loud and hot, it was never meant to run at those clocks.

My point being, AMD can make a chip that's twice, three or even four times as big as the chip in the 5700, under clock and volt it so the temps are easily manageable and they have a 2080 ti beater at $599-699 but sadly they will probably charge more as the competition does but then at least we might have some pricing wars for a while, maybe even until Intel comes along with some more pricing competition. 

All being well AMD will have these chips ready for November, I don't know the time scales nvidia will do 7nm Ampere but I would expect AMD to be slightly faster as they have the 7nm experience and need the cards more. Nvidia might sit back and see what they need to do with Ampere but they will probably make the line up and then simply price accordingly.

Either way, no matter which fanboy camp you hail from the sorely missed competition is long overdue and great news for our wallets.

Let me:

Performance-wise and especially in regards to performance per dollar, the 5700 xt and the 5700 win clearly over nvidia's same price or even higher priced cards. 
The issues are heating and some weird results here and there, because the drivers are not perfected yet and the blower-style fan is garbage.

Or they can not solve the heat problem and you might want to consider going with nvidia after all.

text: @wing0zero  nonsense.  There is no limit to how parallel graphics graphics cards can get.  You can ALWAYS get more speed by having more units calculating pixels at once. author: @joshuascholar3220

text:
@joshuascholar3220  
No it doesn't work totally like that, yeah you can add more units but to keep at the same TDP you would have to slow them like you say, and you would end up at the same TFLOP result when you do, for example a 2080Ti uses more power than a 2080 as it has more SM's,  now if you were to clock the Ti so it was the same power draw as the 2080 it would perform the same even though it has more cores.

Cores x Clock in HZ x FP Operations per clock  / One Trillion, no getting around the math for performance dude, by your logic it would be better to have say double the cores at half the clock speed, then why don't they do that? Because it's pointless and gives the same result with a couple of draw backs too.

So they are peaking with this node and can't do much beyond a 260W 5800XT as the 225W 5700XT can hit 90c+ on their shitty cooler, they would have to release vendor cards only with really good cooling to go much beyond the 5700XT.
author: @wing0zero

text: @wing0zero  that's not true, AMD goes for high clocks, well past the point of diminishing returns on power usage.  It's anything but linear.
author: @joshuascholar3220

text:
@joshuascholar3220  
Performance is always linear as it's math, but yeah power draw can shoot up at the end exponentially, I wouldn't say that is the main problem though, yeah it's hitting 90c on the XT but I doubt a lot of watts is wasted on leakage, when the vendor cards launch with good coolers that probably keep it round the 70c mark at the same clocks I bet power draw isn't that much lower, the problem is probably the stretched to the limit GCN side of the GPU which it's still mainly based on, GCN from the 7000 series onwards has only really gained performance due to die shrinks so they can slap more FP, TMUs and ROPs on, which stems from heavy budget constraints to improve it, although there are genuine architecture improvements this time with Navi it's still not quite there this gen.
author: @wing0zero

text: @wing0zero  people say dumb stuff about graphics cards. While there are limits to how much performance you can get per dollar at any given time, there aren't any limits to the performance of graphics cards in the long run.  It gets me angry when people who should know better say stuff like amdahl's law limits graphics performance.  No, it doesn't because you can always have multiple models to draw from, separate memory and have different processor for different pixels or even for different subpixels.

text:
May anyone explain to me how AMD has better Linux driver support than Nvidia as Anthony mentioned?
personally speaking, I find AMD driver in Linux almost unusable. It doesn't even include basic gpu monitoring feature which NVIDIA provides with nvdia-smi.
author: @kokonato8646

text:
The GUI tweaking and monitoring tools are harder to come by, yes, but those aren't drivers. The drivers are what allow the card to interface with the OS and draw frames on your screen. 


Mesa (the open source amd gpu driver project) is baked in to the kernel (READ: no installation needed!) and consistently has fantastic performance within days of new gpu releases with few regressions and increased stability as a result.

The Nvidia drivers suffer from regressions and performance losses for older GPUs as well as delays for newer ones and are more of a hassle to maintain for linux distros. Not to mention, because they come as binary blobs, they break the unix/linux world's philosophies of free, open collaboration and as a result make it considerably more difficult to integrate them well with the existing ecosystems. Testing and optimizing linux environments for compatibility with nvidia drivers is like trying to shake a closed box and guess what's inside, when you're used to just reaching in and inspecting every item.
